glossary.definition: Discover: Where are the agents? Register: Who owns each identity? Authenticate: Is the identity genuine? Authorize: What can it do? Govern: Can we prove and stop it?

sub names the person on whose behalf a call is made; act names the agent that acts. Delegation keeps both visible: the customer remains the subject while the agent is the actor, and neither impersonates the other.
The OAuth grant that mints a narrower delegated token: audience rebinds to the target resource, scope narrows to what the hop needs, lifetime shortens, and act records the acting agent.

An external agent the customer owns and the enterprise does not control (a consumer AI assistant). The enterprise controls identification, connection, consent and per-tool reach — never the reasoning runtime.
The bounded task an enterprise agent is given: what it may do, what ceiling it must respect, and where it must stop and ask. Enterprise control does not mean unlimited authority.
A high-impact action pauses; approval arrives through a channel the agent does not own (CIBA or MFA); the receipt is bound to the exact intent and consumed once, so a replay is refused.
The correlated audit story: who acted (sub + act), under whose authority (token + policy decision), what ran (protocol, tool), and what can be proved at each lifecycle stage.
The PingOne Privilege brokered entry to a protected MCP tool: a time-bound session is opened, the protected call runs inside it, and the underlying credential never reaches the agent or the browser.
Prompt injection, replay, scope escalation and audience mismatch each stop at a different observable boundary. The model’s mistake cannot manufacture authority.
A detected agent moves from unknown to known (register with an owner) to stopped (revoke). The proof of governance is the next call failing closed.
PingOne Authorize evaluates the action independently of the agent: PERMIT or DENY with a reason and obligations, enforced by the gateway before the tool runs. The agent cannot argue with it.

Agent2Agent task handoff: the primary agent discovers the specialist’s Agent Card and exchanges authority for it. The act chain nests (specialist acts for planner acts for customer) and every hop narrows scope.
Client Initiated Backchannel Authentication: the agent’s high-impact request triggers a push to the customer’s registered channel; approval comes back out-of-band and is bound to the exact intent.
MCP initialize and tools/list tell an agent what a tool is and what schema it accepts. That is discovery evidence; the gateway and policy decision on tools/call is the execution authority.
The human sign-in flow: authorization-code with a code challenge, the exchange done server-side in the BFF, tokens never handed to browser JavaScript.
The backend-for-frontend holds the user’s tokens in the server-side session; the browser holds only an HttpOnly cookie and every downstream hop spends tokens from custody.
Classify before trusting: who owns the agent, where it runs, whose authority it carries. Consumer, enterprise, employee and third-party each get a different control pattern.
The first evidence step: runtime and owner separate a Personal Agent from an Enterprise Agent from an employee agent from a third-party embedded agent.

Client-ID Metadata Discovery: a client identifies itself by publishing metadata at a URL. Demonstrated here as a mock; PingOne does not support CIMD, so DCR or managed registration supplies the metadata.

sources.title: Agent Identity Academy lesson prototype (AI-DEMO2 static Academy, rewritten customer-neutral)
sources.use: The 13 lessons, their actors, frames and evidence shapes.

cards.label: Start: the five lifecycle questions
cards.description: Where are the agents? Who owns each identity? Is the identity genuine? What can it do? Can we prove and stop it?

cards.label: 01. Agent landscape — CIAM and Workforce
cards.description: The audience can name the agent, its owner, and the first enforceable trust boundary.

cards.label: 02. Login, OIDC and PKCE — Human identity
cards.description: The audience sees where PingOne proves the person and where the BFF takes custody of tokens.

cards.label: 03. Delegated access — On-behalf-of access
cards.description: The audience can explain sub, act, audience, and scope without calling delegation impersonation.

cards.label: 04. Personal Agent — Consumer & Partner Agent
cards.description: The audience sees how an unknown external agent becomes a bounded, observable channel to protected tools.

cards.label: 05. Digital Assistant — Enterprise / Workload Agent
cards.description: The audience sees an enterprise agent automate service without inheriting unrestricted customer power.

cards.label: 06. MCP tools — Protected resource access
cards.description: The audience can distinguish an MCP schema from permission to execute it.

cards.label: 07. Authorize decisions — Fine-grained authorization
cards.description: The audience sees a policy reason and the gateway enforce both PERMIT and DENY.

cards.label: 08. Human approval — Consent and step-up
cards.description: The audience sees approval as a cryptographically bounded event, not a checkbox supplied by the agent.

cards.label: 09. A2A delegation — Workload Agent handoff
cards.description: The audience separates A2A conversation mechanics from OAuth authority and policy enforcement.

cards.label: 10. Privilege MCP — Protected MCP session
cards.description: The audience sees secretless privileged execution with a visible start, bounded session, and end.

cards.label: 11. Threat defense — Boundary enforcement
cards.description: The audience sees that model instructions cannot expand identity, scope, audience, or replay rights.

cards.label: 12. Lifecycle and revoke — Unknown to known
cards.description: The audience sees that agent identity has a manageable lifecycle independent of the model runtime.

cards.label: 13. Evidence and products — All five stages
cards.description: The audience can point to proof for who acted, under whose authority, what was allowed, and what happened.

stories.title: Agent landscape
stories.say: Start with classification. The control pattern changes when the customer owns the agent versus when the enterprise owns it.

stories.title: Login, OIDC and PKCE
stories.say: The browser participates in the redirect, but the BFF owns the sensitive exchange and session.

stories.title: Delegated access
stories.say: The customer remains visible in the chain; the agent gains only the authority required for this hop.

stories.title: Personal Agent
stories.say: We do not control the Personal Agent. We control whether it can identify itself, connect, receive consent, and reach each protected tool.

stories.title: Digital Assistant
stories.say: Enterprise control does not mean unlimited authority. The assistant gets a task, a ceiling, and an approval boundary.

stories.title: MCP tools
stories.say: A tool appearing in tools/list is discovery evidence. The later policy decision is execution authority.

stories.title: Authorize decisions
stories.say: The agent may request either action. Only the independently evaluated policy result reaches the protected tool.

stories.title: Human approval
stories.say: The assistant cannot assert that consent exists. The customer proves approval through a separate trusted channel.

stories.title: A2A delegation
stories.say: The Agent Card says how to talk to the specialist. OAuth and policy still decide what that specialist may do.

stories.title: Privilege MCP
stories.say: The agent receives a result, not the credential. Privilege owns the protected connection and its lifetime.

stories.title: Threat defense
stories.say: The lesson is not that the model never makes a mistake. The lesson is that its mistake cannot manufacture authority.

stories.title: Lifecycle and revoke
stories.say: Blocking one call is not lifecycle management. Revocation changes what the identity can do on the next attempt.

stories.title: Evidence and products
stories.say: Close on evidence, not architecture boxes. Every control should answer one customer question and point to its proof.
